9	
10	# ADR-010 — Declare every plan quota in one table
11	
12	## Status
13	
14	Accepted, and stable since it was written: no plan quota anywhere in the
15	product is declared outside `PLAN_LIMITS`, and Rin Saito's billing work
16	since January 2026 has consistently added new consumers of that table
17	rather than new sources of truth.
18	
19	## Context
20	
21	By the second week of January 2026, plan quotas were scattered across at
22	least four places: a hardcoded `10` in the project-create Server Action for
23	starter-plan project limits, a similar hardcoded seat count in the invite
24	flow, a webhook-endpoint-count check that used a different number than the
25	pricing page's marketing copy, and a usage-meter UI component with its own
26	copy of "what does growth include" for rendering a progress bar. None of
27	these agreed with each other after a pricing change in December 2025 bumped
28	starter-plan seats from 8 to 10 — the invite flow's hardcoded check was
29	updated, the usage meter was not, and for two weeks the UI showed a starter
30	org as "8 of 8 seats used" when they in fact had room for two more.
31	
32	Rin Saito, who owns billing and plans, proposed collapsing every quota into
33	one declaration specifically because the bug was not really about seats — it
34	was about there being no way to know, short of grepping the whole codebase,
35	how many places would need to change the next time a plan's limits moved.
36	Four plans (`free`, `starter`, `growth`, `enterprise`) and nine quota-shaped
37	fields per plan meant thirty-six numbers that had to move together every time
38	pricing changed, and pricing was expected to change more than once given the
39	product was pre-launch at the time.
40	
41	## Decision
42	
43	`src/config/plan-limits.ts` declares `PlanLimits` as a single interface —
44	`plan`, `seats`, `projects`, `issuesPerProject`, `storageMb`,
45	`apiRequestsPerHour`, `webhooks`, `retentionDays`, `includedFlags`,
46	`priceCentsPerSeatMonthly` — and `PLAN_LIMITS` as a `Readonly<Record<PlanId,
47	PlanLimits>>` covering all four plans completely: free (3 seats, 2 projects,
48	100 issues/project, 100 MB storage, 100 API req/hr, 0 webhooks, 30-day
49	retention, free price), starter (10/10/1,000/2,000/1,000/2/90 days/$9.00 per
50	seat), growth (50/100/10,000/20,000/10,000/10/365 days/$19.00 per seat), and
51	enterprise (unlimited seats, projects, and issues per project, 500,000 MB
52	storage, 100,000 API req/hr, unlimited webhooks, 2,555-day retention,
53	$39.00 per seat). `UNLIMITED` is declared once as `Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY`
54	and used everywhere a quota has no ceiling — REQ-137 requires unlimited be
55	represented this way specifically so downstream arithmetic (`used + requested
56	> limit`) behaves correctly without a special-cased "is this unlimited"
57	branch scattered through call sites.
58	
59	Every consumer reads through one of four functions, never the `PLAN_LIMITS`
60	table directly, and the module's own documentation states this explicitly:
61	adding a field to `PlanLimits` ripples into every one of these call sites,
62	and that ripple is intentional. `getPlanLimits(plan)` returns the whole
63	object; `getLimit(plan, resource)` reads one numeric quota by
64	`LimitedResource` key without the caller destructuring the whole
65	`PlanLimits` shape; `planAtLeast(plan, minPlan)` compares two plans by their
66	position in `PLAN_ORDER` (`free < starter < growth < enterprise`), used both
67	by billing logic and, via ADR-012, by plan-gated feature flags;
68	`wouldExceedLimit(plan, resource, used, requested = 1)` is the single
69	predicate every quota-check call site uses to decide whether an action would
70	breach a limit, rather than each call site writing its own `used + 1 >
71	limit` comparison. The known consumers, per the module's own comment, are
72	`BillingService`, the invite flow, the project-create action, the webhook
73	settings page, the usage meter component, and the seat-limit job — six
74	independent features, all reading the same nine numbers.
75	
76	## Consequences
77	
78	**What this buys the team.** A pricing change is now a single-file edit:
79	when growth-plan webhook endpoints went from 5 to 10 in February 2026 (a
80	real change, prompted by Kaya Ferreira's webhook usage data showing
81	customers routinely hitting the old ceiling), it touched exactly one line in
82	`plan-limits.ts` and nothing else — the usage meter, the webhook settings
83	page, and the plan-limit-exceeded error message all picked up the new number
84	automatically because none of them stored their own copy. `wouldExceedLimit()`
85	being the one predicate everywhere also means REQ-138 (exceeding a quota
86	produces `plan_limit_exceeded`, not a crash) is satisfied uniformly: every
87	quota check goes through the same function, so there is one place to verify
88	the error path is correct, not nine. `UNLIMITED` as `Infinity` specifically
89	means an enterprise org's `wouldExceedLimit(plan, "seats", 50_000, 1)` call
90	returns `false` through ordinary floating-point comparison, with no
91	`if (limit === UNLIMITED) return false` special case anywhere — REQ-137's
92	requirement turned into a genuine simplification rather than an extra branch.
93	
94	**What it costs.** Every quota-dependent feature now has a hard dependency on
95	this one module, which means `plan-limits.ts` cannot be changed casually — a
96	change to the `PlanLimits` interface shape (adding a tenth field, say, for a
97	new resource type) is a breaking change for every one of its six known
98	consumers simultaneously, and each has to be updated in the same pull
99	request or the build fails typechecking. This is the ripple the module's
100	documentation calls out as intentional, but it means plan-limits changes are
101	reviewed more heavily than an average config edit — Rin Saito's team treats
102	any diff touching this file as requiring a second reviewer from billing,
103	independent of the size of the diff. The table also has no notion of
104	grandfathering or per-organization overrides built in: an organization
105	negotiated a custom seat count outside the four standard plans has no
106	representation in this model today, which is a known gap the sales team has
107	flagged and which would require either a fifth synthetic "plan" or a
108	per-org override layered on top of `PLAN_LIMITS` — not yet built, and
109	explicitly out of scope for this ADR.
110	
111	## Alternatives considered
112	
113	**Quotas stored in the database, editable without a deploy.** Attractive for
114	operational flexibility (support could adjust a struggling customer's limits
115	without engineering involvement) but rejected for the initial build: it adds
116	a runtime dependency (a database round trip) to every quota check, in a
117	codebase that otherwise keeps configuration-shaped data as static
118	TypeScript, and it removes the compile-time guarantee that every `PlanId`
119	has a complete `PlanLimits` record — a missing row in a database table fails
120	at runtime, a missing key in a `Record<PlanId, PlanLimits>` fails
121	typechecking. The team left the door open to a database-backed override
122	layer sitting on top of this table later, without abandoning the table
123	itself as the base declaration.
124	
125	**Quotas colocated with each feature** (the webhook module declares its own
126	webhook-count limits, the project module its own project-count limits, and
127	so on). This is close to what the codebase organically had before this ADR,
128	and it is exactly what produced the seat-count drift bug — rejected for the
129	same reason ADR-003 rejects per-resource authorization guards: no single
130	place to see or change the whole quota picture at once.
131	
132	**Environment-variable-driven quotas**, one env var per plan per resource.
133	Rejected as unwieldy at thirty-six values, unable to express the
134	`includedFlags` array cleanly, and — in an offline, no-external-config-store
135	environment — no real operational benefit over a TypeScript constant that is
136	already deployed with the application and reviewed like any other code
137	change.
138	
139	## References
140	
141	- REQ-131 (four plans form an ordered ladder), REQ-132 (plan quotas declared
142	  in one place), REQ-137 (unlimited represented by positive infinity),
143	  REQ-138 (exceeding a quota produces `plan_limit_exceeded`, not a crash)
144	- ADR-011 (the rate limiter reads `apiRequestsPerHour` from this same table
145	  to scale bucket capacity), ADR-012 (plan-gated feature flags compare
146	  against `PLAN_ORDER` via `planAtLeast`)
147	- Code: `src/config/plan-limits.ts` (`PlanLimits`, `PLAN_LIMITS`,
148	  `PLAN_ORDER`, `UNLIMITED`, `getPlanLimits`, `getLimit`, `planAtLeast`,
149	  `wouldExceedLimit`), `src/types/billing.ts` (`LimitedResource`, `PlanId`)
150

$39.00 per seat). `UNLIMITED` is declared once as `Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY`
and used everywhere a quota has no ceiling — REQ-137 requires unlimited be
represented this way specifically so downstream arithmetic (`used + requested
> limit`) behaves correctly without a special-cased "is this unlimited"
branch scattered through call sites.

Every consumer reads through one of four functions, never the `PLAN_LIMITS`
table directly, and the module's own documentation states this explicitly:
adding a field to `PlanLimits` ripples into every one of these call sites,
and that ripple is intentional. `getPlanLimits(plan)` returns the whole
object; `getLimit(plan, resource)` reads one numeric quota by
`LimitedResource` key without the caller destructuring the whole
`PlanLimits` shape; `planAtLeast(plan, minPlan)` compares two plans by their
position in `PLAN_ORDER` (`free < starter < growth < enterprise`), used both
by billing logic and, via ADR-012, by plan-gated feature flags;
`wouldExceedLimit(plan, resource, used, requested = 1)` is the single
predicate every quota-check call site uses to decide whether an action would
breach a limit, rather than each call site writing its own `used + 1 >
limit` comparison. The known consumers, per the module's own comment, are
`BillingService`, the invite flow, the project-create action, the webhook
settings page, the usage meter component, and the seat-limit job — six
independent features, all reading the same nine numbers.

## Consequences

**What this buys the team.** A pricing change is now a single-file edit:
when growth-plan webhook endpoints went from 5 to 10 in February 2026 (a
real change, prompted by Kaya Ferreira's webhook usage data showing
customers routinely hitting the old ceiling), it touched exactly one line in
`plan-limits.ts` and nothing else — the usage meter, the webhook settings
page, and the plan-limit-exceeded error message all picked up the new number
automatically because none of them stored their own copy. `wouldExceedLimit()`
being the one predicate everywhere also means REQ-138 (exceeding a quota
produces `plan_limit_exceeded`, not a crash) is satisfied uniformly: every
quota check goes through the same function, so there is one place to verify
the error path is correct, not nine. `UNLIMITED` as `Infinity` specifically
means an enterprise org's `wouldExceedLimit(plan, "seats", 50_000, 1)` call
returns `false` through ordinary floating-point comparison, with no
`if (limit === UNLIMITED) return false` special case anywhere — REQ-137's
requirement turned into a genuine simplification rather than an extra branch.

**What it costs.** Every quota-dependent feature now has a hard dependency on
this one module, which means `plan-limits.ts` cannot be changed casually — a
change to the `PlanLimits` interface shape (adding a tenth field, say, for a
new resource type) is a breaking change for every one of its six known
consumers simultaneously, and each has to be updated in the same pull
request or the build fails typechecking. This is the ripple the module's
documentation calls out as intentional, but it means plan-limits changes are
reviewed more heavily than an average config edit — Rin Saito's team treats
any diff touching this file as requiring a second reviewer from billing,
independent of the size of the diff. The table also has no notion of
grandfathering or per-organization overrides built in: an organization
negotiated a custom seat count outside the four standard plans has no
representation in this model today, which is a known gap the sales team has
flagged and which would require either a fifth synthetic "plan" or a
per-org override layered on top of `PLAN_LIMITS` — not yet built, and
explicitly out of scope for this ADR.

## Alternatives considered

**Quotas stored in the database, editable without a deploy.** Attractive for
operational flexibility (support could adjust a struggling customer's limits
without engineering involvement) but rejected for the initial build: it adds
a runtime dependency (a database round trip) to every quota check, in a
codebase that otherwise keeps configuration-shaped data as static
TypeScript, and it removes the compile-time guarantee that every `PlanId`
has a complete `PlanLimits` record — a missing row in a database table fails
at runtime, a missing key in a `Record<PlanId, PlanLimits>` fails
typechecking. The team left the door open to a database-backed override
layer sitting on top of this table later, without abandoning the table
itself as the base declaration.

**Quotas colocated with each feature** (the webhook module declares its own
webhook-count limits, the project module its own project-count limits, and
so on). This is close to what the codebase organically had before this ADR,
and it is exactly what produced the seat-count drift bug — rejected for the
same reason ADR-003 rejects per-resource authorization guards: no single
place to see or change the whole quota picture at once.

**Environment-variable-driven quotas**, one env var per plan per resource.
Rejected as unwieldy at thirty-six values, unable to express the
`includedFlags` array cleanly, and — in an offline, no-external-config-store
environment — no real operational benefit over a TypeScript constant that is
already deployed with the application and reviewed like any other code
change.

## References

- REQ-131 (four plans form an ordered ladder), REQ-132 (plan quotas declared
  in one place), REQ-137 (unlimited represented by positive infinity),
  REQ-138 (exceeding a quota produces `plan_limit_exceeded`, not a crash)
- ADR-011 (the rate limiter reads `apiRequestsPerHour` from this same table
  to scale bucket capacity), ADR-012 (plan-gated feature flags compare
  against `PLAN_ORDER` via `planAtLeast`)
- Code: `src/config/plan-limits.ts` (`PlanLimits`, `PLAN_LIMITS`,
  `PLAN_ORDER`, `UNLIMITED`, `getPlanLimits`, `getLimit`, `planAtLeast`,
  `wouldExceedLimit`), `src/types/billing.ts` (`LimitedResource`, `PlanId`)

10	# ADR-011 — An in-process token-bucket rate limiter
11	
12	## Status
13	
14	Accepted. In production use for member invites, comment creation, issue
15	creation, search queries, password resets, and webhook delivery since late
16	January 2026, with no changes to its core algorithm since.
17	
18	## Context
19	
20	By mid-January 2026, several independent features needed rate limiting for
21	different, unrelated reasons: REQ-096 requires comment creation be rate
22	limited per organization (to blunt a scripted mention-spam scenario Kaya
23	Ferreira had reproduced in testing), REQ-176 requires search queries be rate
24	limited per organization (the search index's `LIKE`-based matching, see
25	ADR-017, is not free, and an unthrottled query loop could degrade the whole
26	database for every organization sharing the process), REQ-208 requires
27	password-reset requests be rate limited (a standard account-enumeration and
28	abuse defense), and REQ-161 requires webhook delivery itself be rate limited
29	per organization, distinct from the retry backoff ADR-018 governs.
30	
31	The same offline, single-process, no-external-services constraint that
32	shaped ADR-005 and ADR-002 applied here too: there was no Redis or managed
33	rate-limiting service to point at, and the team wanted one limiter
34	implementation, not five bespoke ones each reinventing token-bucket or
35	fixed-window math with its own bugs. There was also a fairness concern
36	specific to Taskflow's plan model: a flat rate limit applied equally to a
37	free-plan org and an enterprise-plan org would either be too generous for
38	free (defeating the point) or too strict for enterprise (an org paying for
39	100,000 API requests per hour should not be capped at the same comment-
40	creation rate as a three-seat free org).
41	
42	## Decision
43	
44	`src/lib/rate-limit.ts` implements a token-bucket limiter keyed by
45	`(orgId, bucketKey)`, held entirely in an in-process `Map`, matching the
46	event bus's in-process model from ADR-005 and for the identical reason:
47	Taskflow runs single-writer with no external cache to hold this state
48	instead. `RATE_LIMIT_BUCKETS` declares the base shape (`capacity`,
49	`refillPerMinute`) per named bucket — `member:invite` (20 capacity, 2/min
50	refill), `comment:create` (60, 20), `issue:create` (60, 20), `search:query`
51	(120, 60), `auth:password-reset` (5, 1), `webhook:deliver` (100, 50) — with
52	`DEFAULT_BUCKET` (30, 10) applied to any key not in the table.
53	
54	Bucket size is not fixed, though: `configFor(orgId, bucketKey)` scales the
55	base config by the org's plan, reading `apiRequestsPerHour` from
56	`getPlanLimits()` in ADR-010's plan-limits table — the module's own
57	documentation states this is deliberate, so "the limiter and the plan
58	catalogue can never drift apart: the plan is the source of the ceiling, this
59	table only sets the relative shape." The scale factor is
60	`max(1, hourly / 100)`, capped so no bucket can scale beyond 100x its base
61	size regardless of how generous a plan's hourly allowance is — this cap
62	exists specifically so a mis-declared or future extremely-high-allowance plan
63	cannot produce a bucket so large it stops meaningfully limiting anything.
64	`setOrgPlan(orgId, plan)` is how a service records an org's plan so
65	subsequent `consumeRateLimit()` calls for that org scale correctly; it is
66	called wherever a service already has the org's plan loaded, rather than the
67	limiter looking it up itself.
68	
69	`consumeRateLimit(orgId, bucketKey, cost = 1)` is the sole entry point.
70	Async by contract — the module's documentation notes this is deliberate,
71	"the production limiter is expected to move behind a store" eventually, and
72	every call site already awaits it, so promoting the current in-memory
73	implementation to a persisted one later would not change any caller. It
74	refills tokens for elapsed time since the bucket's last touch, then spends
75	`cost` tokens if enough are available, returning a `RateLimitVerdict`
76	(`allowed`, `remaining`, `resetAt`) — `resetAt` is computed from the deficit
77	and the refill rate, giving callers (and, via `toAppError()`'s
78	`rate_limited` code, HTTP 429 responses) a concrete "try again after" time
79	rather than a bare rejection. `resetRateLimits()` exists for tests, and
80	`getBucketConfig(bucketKey)` exposes the base (unscaled) config for callers
81	that need to display a limit's shape (e.g. account settings) without
82	performing a consume.
83	
84	## Consequences
85	
86	**What this buys the team.** Six otherwise-unrelated features — invites,
87	comments, issue creation, search, password reset, webhook delivery — share
88	one algorithm, one verdict shape, and one plan-scaling rule, so a bug fix or
89	a behavioral change in `consumeRateLimit()` benefits all six at once, and a
90	new rate-limited feature is a one-line addition to `RATE_LIMIT_BUCKETS` plus
91	a `consumeRateLimit()` call at the right point in the service, not a new
92	implementation. Because bucket capacity scales from the same `PlanLimits`
93	table ADR-010 declares, there is no separate "rate limit tier" concept to
94	keep in sync with the plan ladder — an enterprise org's generous
95	`apiRequestsPerHour` automatically widens every rate-limited action's bucket
96	proportionally, with no second config surface for pricing to reason about.
97	The `RateLimitVerdict`'s `resetAt` has made the product-facing error message
98	concretely better than a bare "try again later" — the search dialog and the
99	comment composer both surface the actual reset time.
100	
101	**What it costs.** State lives in a plain `Map` in one process's memory,
102	which means it does not survive a process restart (every bucket resets to
103	full on deploy, a mild and accepted leniency) and, more importantly, does
104	not coordinate across multiple processes — if Taskflow were ever deployed
105	behind more than one application instance sharing a database, each instance
106	would enforce its own independent rate limit, meaning the effective limit an
107	organization experiences would be the configured limit multiplied by the
108	number of instances. This is an explicit, accepted constraint of the
109	single-writer, single-process deployment model the whole corpus assumes, not
110	an oversight; the module's own "expected to move behind a store" comment,
111	and the fact that every call site already treats `consumeRateLimit` as async,
112	is the team's acknowledgment that this would need to change before a
113	multi-instance deployment. The 100x scaling cap also means a hypothetical
114	future plan with an enormous `apiRequestsPerHour` allowance would not get a
115	correspondingly enormous comment-creation bucket — this is intentional
116	(comment creation should never be effectively unlimited regardless of plan)
117	but it does mean `apiRequestsPerHour` is not a perfectly literal ceiling on
118	every rate-limited action; it is a scaling input, and that distinction has
119	had to be explained to product stakeholders more than once when they
120	compared advertised API limits against observed comment-rate behavior.
121	
122	## Alternatives considered
123	
124	**A fixed-window counter instead of token bucket.** Simpler to implement and
125	reason about, but rejected because fixed windows allow a burst at the
126	boundary between two windows (2x the intended rate in the worst case, all at
127	the window edge) that token buckets smooth out naturally through continuous
128	refill — a meaningful difference for the abuse-prevention use cases (password
129	reset, comment spam) this limiter primarily exists to serve.
130	
131	**An external rate-limiting service or Redis-backed sliding window.** The
132	production-grade answer for a multi-instance deployment, and the natural
133	next step if Taskflow ever needs one, but ruled out for the same
134	no-external-services reason as ADR-005's event bus and ADR-002's database
135	choice — there is nothing to point it at in this environment.
136	
137	**A single global limit per organization**, rather than one bucket per
138	`(orgId, bucketKey)`. Rejected because it would let a burst of search
139	queries exhaust the same budget as password-reset attempts, defeating the
140	point of rate limiting each abuse scenario independently — a user
141	legitimately searching heavily should not accidentally lock themselves out
142	of resetting their password.
143	
144	## References
145	
146	- REQ-096 (comment creation rate limited per organization), REQ-161 (webhook
147	  delivery rate limited per organization), REQ-176 (search queries rate
148	  limited per organization), REQ-208 (password reset rate limited)
149	- ADR-005 (the in-process, single-process model this limiter's state storage
150	  mirrors, for the same environmental reasons), ADR-010 (`PlanLimits` is the
151	  source the limiter scales bucket capacity from)
152	- Code: `src/lib/rate-limit.ts` (`consumeRateLimit`, `getBucketConfig`,
153	  `setOrgPlan`, `resetRateLimits`, `RateLimitVerdict`, `RATE_LIMIT_BUCKETS`,
154	  `DEFAULT_BUCKET`), `src/config/plan-limits.ts` (`getPlanLimits`)

# ADR-011 — An in-process token-bucket rate limiter

## Status

implementation, not five bespoke ones each reinventing token-bucket or
fixed-window math with its own bugs. There was also a fairness concern

free-plan org and an enterprise-plan org would either be too generous for
free (defeating the point) or too strict for enterprise (an org paying for
100,000 API requests per hour should not be capped at the same comment-
creation rate as a three-seat free org).

event bus's in-process model from ADR-005 and for the identical reason:

and the refill rate, giving callers (and, via `toAppError()`'s

rather than a bare rejection. `resetRateLimits()` exists for tests, and
`getBucketConfig(bucketKey)` exposes the base (unscaled) config for callers
that need to display a limit's shape (e.g. account settings) without
performing a consume.

## Consequences

**What this buys the team.** Six otherwise-unrelated features — invites,
comments, issue creation, search, password reset, webhook delivery — share

keep in sync with the plan ladder — an enterprise org's generous

proportionally, with no second config surface for pricing to reason about.
The `RateLimitVerdict`'s `resetAt` has made the product-facing error message
concretely better than a bare "try again later" — the search dialog and the

and the fact that every call site already treats `consumeRateLimit` as async,

2	title: Map domain error classes onto a closed error code union
3	id: ADR-014
4	status: accepted
5	owners: [platform-team]
6	last_updated: 2026-02-19
7	related: [REQ-138, ADR-003, ADR-004, ADR-009, ADR-012]
8	---
9	
10	# ADR-014 — Map domain error classes onto a closed error code union
11	
12	## Status
13	
14	Accepted, and treated as the mandatory error-handling contract for every
15	Server Action and Route Handler in the product — no mutation path is exempt.
16	
17	## Context
18	
19	Before this ADR, in December 2025 and January 2026, error handling in
20	Server Actions was ad hoc: some caught specific error classes and returned a
21	tailored message, some let errors propagate raw (which, in the App Router,
22	meant a generic Next.js error boundary rendering "something went wrong" with
23	no field-level detail), and none agreed on an HTTP-status-equivalent code the
24	client could branch on. This became a concrete product problem once REQ-138
25	was written — "exceeding a quota produces `plan_limit_exceeded`, not a
26	crash" — because at the time there was no `plan_limit_exceeded` concept
27	anywhere in the code; a quota breach was just a thrown `Error` with a plain
28	string message, indistinguishable, from the client's point of view, from any
29	other unexpected failure.
30	
31	By that point the domain layer already had several purpose-built error
32	classes serving different concerns — `PermissionDeniedError` from ADR-003,
33	`TenantScopeError` from ADR-006, `AlreadyArchivedError` from ADR-004, plus
34	`FeatureDisabledError` (ADR-012) and `InvalidSlugError` (slug validation) —
35	each thrown from its own module, each carrying different, useful metadata
36	(`PermissionDeniedError` carries the denied `action` and the `reason` code
37	from `explain()`; `TenantScopeError` carries the expected and actual
38	`orgId`). The team needed a single place that turned any of these, plus
39	Zod's own `ZodError` from ADR-009, into one closed, predictable client-facing
40	shape, without each Server Action re-implementing that translation.
41	
42	## Decision
43	
44	`src/lib/errors.ts` defines `HTTP_STATUS_BY_CODE`, a
45	`Readonly<Record<ErrorCode, number>>` covering exactly nine codes:
46	`unauthorized` (401), `forbidden` (403), `not_found` (404),
47	`validation_failed` (422), `conflict` (409), `rate_limited` (429),
48	`plan_limit_exceeded` (402), `tenant_scope_violation` (403), and
49	`internal_error` (500). This is a closed union — `ErrorCode` in
50	`src/types/api.ts` — and every domain error the service layer is permitted to
51	throw maps onto exactly one of these codes, never a raw string.
52	
53	`isDomainError(error)` recognizes the known, deliberately-thrown classes:
54	`PermissionDeniedError`, `TenantScopeError`, `FeatureDisabledError`,
55	`AlreadyArchivedError`, `InvalidSlugError`, and `ZodError` — the module's own
56	documentation states these are the error classes "this module knows how to
57	translate faithfully," implying, correctly, that anything else is treated as
58	an unexpected internal failure. `toAppError(error)` is the actual mapping
59	function: `ZodError` becomes `validation_failed` with `fieldErrorsFromZod()`
60	populating per-field messages; `PermissionDeniedError` becomes `forbidden`
61	with `meta` carrying the denied action, resource kind, and `explain()`
62	reason code (`denied_cross_tenant`, `denied_by_role`, and so on) so a client
63	that wants to log or display *why* access was denied can, without
64	re-deriving it; `TenantScopeError` becomes `tenant_scope_violation` with the
65	expected and actual org ids in `meta`; `FeatureDisabledError` becomes
66	`forbidden` with the flag key; `AlreadyArchivedError` becomes `conflict` with
67	the entity and id; `InvalidSlugError` becomes `validation_failed` with a
68	`slug` field error. Anything not recognized by `isDomainError()` falls
69	through to `internal_error`, with the raw `Error.message` surfaced only if
70	the thrown value actually was an `Error` instance, otherwise a fixed generic
71	string — deliberately not leaking arbitrary thrown values (a string, an
72	object, whatever a third-party dependency might throw) to the client
73	verbatim.
74	
75	`toActionResult(error)` wraps `toAppError()`'s output into the failure half of
76	the `ActionResult<T>` discriminated union every Server Action returns
77	(`{ ok: false, error, submittedAt }`), which is what `withAction()`
78	(`src/actions/_lib/with-action.ts`, ADR-013) calls in its catch block, so an
79	individual Server Action's own code never needs a try/catch around its

title: Map domain error classes onto a closed error code union
id: ADR-014
status: accepted
owners: [platform-team]
last_updated: 2026-02-19
related: [REQ-138, ADR-003, ADR-004, ADR-009, ADR-012]

# ADR-014 — Map domain error classes onto a closed error code union

## Status

Accepted, and treated as the mandatory error-handling contract for every
Server Action and Route Handler in the product — no mutation path is exempt.

## Context

Before this ADR, in December 2025 and January 2026, error handling in
Server Actions was ad hoc: some caught specific error classes and returned a
tailored message, some let errors propagate raw (which, in the App Router,
meant a generic Next.js error boundary rendering "something went wrong" with
no field-level detail), and none agreed on an HTTP-status-equivalent code the
client could branch on. This became a concrete product problem once REQ-138
was written — "exceeding a quota produces `plan_limit_exceeded`, not a
crash" — because at the time there was no `plan_limit_exceeded` concept
anywhere in the code; a quota breach was just a thrown `Error` with a plain
string message, indistinguishable, from the client's point of view, from any
other unexpected failure.

By that point the domain layer already had several purpose-built error
classes serving different concerns — `PermissionDeniedError` from ADR-003,
`TenantScopeError` from ADR-006, `AlreadyArchivedError` from ADR-004, plus
`FeatureDisabledError` (ADR-012) and `InvalidSlugError` (slug validation) —
each thrown from its own module, each carrying different, useful metadata
(`PermissionDeniedError` carries the denied `action` and the `reason` code
from `explain()`; `TenantScopeError` carries the expected and actual
`orgId`). The team needed a single place that turned any of these, plus
Zod's own `ZodError` from ADR-009, into one closed, predictable client-facing
shape, without each Server Action re-implementing that translation.

## Decision

`src/lib/errors.ts` defines `HTTP_STATUS_BY_CODE`, a
`Readonly<Record<ErrorCode, number>>` covering exactly nine codes:
`unauthorized` (401), `forbidden` (403), `not_found` (404),
`validation_failed` (422), `conflict` (409), `rate_limited` (429),
`plan_limit_exceeded` (402), `tenant_scope_violation` (403), and
`internal_error` (500). This is a closed union — `ErrorCode` in
`src/types/api.ts` — and every domain error the service layer is permitted to
throw maps onto exactly one of these codes, never a raw string.

`isDomainError(error)` recognizes the known, deliberately-thrown classes:
`PermissionDeniedError`, `TenantScopeError`, `FeatureDisabledError`,
`AlreadyArchivedError`, `InvalidSlugError`, and `ZodError` — the module's own
documentation states these are the error classes "this module knows how to
translate faithfully," implying, correctly, that anything else is treated as
an unexpected internal failure. `toAppError(error)` is the actual mapping
function: `ZodError` becomes `validation_failed` with `fieldErrorsFromZod()`
populating per-field messages; `PermissionDeniedError` becomes `forbidden`
with `meta` carrying the denied action, resource kind, and `explain()`
reason code (`denied_cross_tenant`, `denied_by_role`, and so on) so a client
that wants to log or display *why* access was denied can, without
re-deriving it; `TenantScopeError` becomes `tenant_scope_violation` with the
expected and actual org ids in `meta`; `FeatureDisabledError` becomes
`forbidden` with the flag key; `AlreadyArchivedError` becomes `conflict` with
the entity and id; `InvalidSlugError` becomes `validation_failed` with a
`slug` field error. Anything not recognized by `isDomainError()` falls
through to `internal_error`, with the raw `Error.message` surfaced only if
the thrown value actually was an `Error` instance, otherwise a fixed generic
string — deliberately not leaking arbitrary thrown values (a string, an
object, whatever a third-party dependency might throw) to the client
verbatim.

`toActionResult(error)` wraps `toAppError()`'s output into the failure half of
the `ActionResult<T>` discriminated union every Server Action returns
(`{ ok: false, error, submittedAt }`), which is what `withAction()`
(`src/actions/_lib/with-action.ts`, ADR-013) calls in its catch block, so an
individual Server Action's own code never needs a try/catch around its
service call at all — the wrapper is where errors become results.

## Consequences

**What this buys the team.** REQ-138 is now trivially true by construction:
a billing quota check throws a plain `Error` today (there is no
`PlanLimitExceededError` class yet — a known gap, see below), but every
*other* domain concern already has a precise code, and the pattern this ADR
establishes is exactly what a future `PlanLimitExceededError` would slot
into. Every client-facing error the product produces now has a stable,
finite vocabulary of nine codes, which makes client-side error handling
(toast messages, inline field errors, redirect-to-login on `unauthorized`)
a matter of switching on `code`, not on parsing message strings. The `meta`
payloads turned into a real debugging and support tool — Jan Novak's SRE
runbooks reference `TenantScopeError`'s `meta.expectedOrgId` /
`meta.actualOrgId` fields directly when triaging a reported cross-tenant
access attempt, because the error itself carries the two org ids that
matter rather than requiring a log correlation exercise.

**What it costs, and what remains a gap.** The mapping function has to be
extended every time a new domain error class is introduced, and forgetting
to do so means the new error class falls through to `internal_error` — safe
in the sense that it does not leak detail, but unhelpful in the sense that a
genuinely expected, recoverable condition (a plan-limit breach, today) gets
treated identically to a genuine bug. This is the concrete, currently-live
gap: `wouldExceedLimit()` (ADR-010) is called by billing-adjacent code, but
nothing yet throws a dedicated `PlanLimitExceededError` that `toAppError()`
recognizes — REQ-139's requirement that quota breaches emit
`billing.limit_exceeded` is satisfied at the event-bus level (ADR-005), but
the *error* a blocked mutation returns to the client today is a generic
`Error`, mapped to `internal_error`, not the `plan_limit_exceeded` code this
ADR's own status table already reserves for it. The platform team has this
tracked as follow-up work, not disputed as a design question — the code and
the HTTP status already exist in `HTTP_STATUS_BY_CODE`, waiting for the
corresponding error class.

## Alternatives considered

**Let each Server Action catch and translate errors itself.** This is what
the codebase had before, and it produced exactly the inconsistency (some
actions detailed, some generic, none agreeing on codes) that motivated this
ADR. Rejected for the same "one place to look, one place to change" reasoning
behind ADR-003 and ADR-010.

**An open-ended error code space** (any string the throwing code chooses,
rather than a closed nine-value union). Rejected because it removes the
guarantee that `HTTP_STATUS_BY_CODE` is exhaustive — a client branching on
`error.code` would have no compile-time assurance it had handled every
possible value, and a new ad hoc code introduced by one Server Action could
silently have no corresponding HTTP status mapping anywhere.

**Encode the error code inside the HTTP status alone**, without a separate
`ErrorCode` string, relying on the numeric status for client branching.
Rejected because two of the nine codes intentionally share an HTTP status
(`forbidden` and `tenant_scope_violation` are both 403) but mean genuinely
different things to the client — a tenant-scope violation should probably
never be retried or reported the same way a permission denial is, even
though both are "403" at the transport level.

## References

- REQ-138 (exceeding a quota produces `plan_limit_exceeded`, not a crash —
  the currently-incomplete case this ADR documents honestly)
- ADR-003 (`PermissionDeniedError`, mapped here to `forbidden`), ADR-004
  (`AlreadyArchivedError`, mapped here to `conflict`), ADR-009 (`ZodError`,
  mapped here to `validation_failed`), ADR-012 (`FeatureDisabledError`,
  mapped here to `forbidden`)
- Code: `src/lib/errors.ts` (`HTTP_STATUS_BY_CODE`, `isDomainError`,
  `toAppError`, `fieldErrorsFromZod`, `toActionResult`), `src/types/api.ts`
  (`ErrorCode`, `ActionResult`, `AppErrorShape`),
  `src/actions/_lib/with-action.ts`

2	title: Four feature flag strategies and one evaluator
3	id: ADR-012
4	status: accepted
5	owners: [platform-team, a.whitfield]
6	last_updated: 2026-02-05

9	
10	# ADR-012 — Four feature flag strategies and one evaluator
11	
12	## Status
13	
14	Accepted, and unmodified since February 2026 apart from new flag entries
15	being added to the registry (ten flags as of this writing). No fifth
16	strategy kind has been proposed.
17	
18	## Context
19	
20	By late January 2026, Taskflow needed feature flags for genuinely different
21	reasons: `kanban_board` and `csv_export` gate a feature behind a plan tier;
22	`ai_issue_summary` needed a gradual, controlled rollout to a percentage of
23	organizations before committing to it product-wide; `issue_templates` was a
24	feature the team wanted available to admins only, regardless of plan, while
25	it was still being validated with early customers; and `command_palette` was
26	simply a flag the team wanted to be able to kill in an emergency without
27	being tied to any of the above conditions, always on unless someone flips it
28	off. Ada Whitfield, as product manager, pushed for these to be genuinely
29	independent knobs rather than one mechanism awkwardly repurposed for all four
30	— a plan-gate reused to fake a percentage rollout (by, say, defining a fake
31	plan tier) would have been legible to nobody maintaining the pricing page.
32	
33	The team also wanted exactly one function anyone could call to ask "is this
34	flag on," used identically by server code deciding whether to execute a
35	gated code path and by the client UI deciding whether to render a gated
36	control — with no risk of the two disagreeing, which would show a control
37	the server would then reject, or hide a control the server would have
38	allowed. This mirrors the reasoning behind ADR-003's single permission entry
39	point directly: a scattered set of ad hoc "is this org on the growth plan"
40	checks sprinkled through the UI was judged the same kind of drift risk as
41	scattered role checks.
42	
43	## Decision
44	
45	`src/config/feature-flags.ts` declares `FEATURE_FLAG_DEFINITIONS`, a
46	`Readonly<Record<FeatureFlagKey, FeatureFlagDefinition>>` — REQ-195's closed
47	union of flag keys — where each definition carries a `strategy` of exactly
48	one of four kinds:
49	
50	- `{ kind: "off" }` / `{ kind: "on" }` — unconditional. `command_palette` uses
51	  `"on"`, and is the one flag in the registry marked `overridable: false`
52	  since there is no plan or role condition to override in the first place
53	  that would make an override meaningful.
54	- `{ kind: "plan", minPlan }` — gated by `planAtLeast(ctx.plan, minPlan)`,
55	  reading directly from ADR-010's `PLAN_ORDER`. `kanban_board` (starter),
56	  `activity_feed` and `digest_email` and `webhooks` (growth), and
57	  `public_projects` and `advanced_search` (enterprise) all use this
58	  strategy.
59	- `{ kind: "role", minRole }` — gated by `ROLE_RANK[ctx.role] >=
60	  ROLE_RANK[minRole]`, reading the same role-rank table ADR-003's
61	  authorization decision uses. `issue_templates` (admin) is the one flag
62	  using this strategy today.
63	- `{ kind: "percentage", percent }` — a deterministic bucket, not a random
64	  roll per request: `bucketOf(flag, ctx)` FNV-1a-hashes the string
65	  `"${flag}:${orgId}:${userId}"` into a 0-99 bucket, and the flag is enabled
66	  if that bucket is below `percent`. `ai_issue_summary` is set at 25 percent.
67	  Determinism matters specifically so REQ-189 (percentage rollout is
68	  deterministic per organization) holds — a given org, or a given
69	  user-in-org, sees the same on/off answer on every request, never a flicker
70	  between page loads.
71	
72	`isEnabled(flag, ctx)` in `src/lib/feature-flags.ts` is the sole evaluator.
73	It checks `definition.overridable && ctx.overrides?.includes(flag)` first —
74	REQ-191's per-organization override, stored in organization settings and
75	passed through the `FlagContext` — before falling through to the strategy
76	switch; `command_palette` and `webhooks` are the two flags marked
77	non-overridable (REQ-190), meaning an org cannot self-enable webhooks by
78	override alone even if it were somehow added to their settings, since
79	`webhooks` also requires the `growth` plan strategy to pass and overrides for
80	it are explicitly disabled at the definition level. `snapshotFlags(ctx)`
81	evaluates every flag at once and is what the dashboard layout serializes into
82	the client-side flag provider — REQ-194's requirement that the client
83	receives a flag snapshot, not the registry, meaning the client never sees
84	`FEATURE_FLAG_DEFINITIONS` itself, only the boolean outcome for the current
85	context, so a client cannot infer a competitor's rollout percentage or a
86	gated flag's exact plan requirement from inspecting the bundle.
87	`assertEnabled(flag, ctx)` is the throwing guard, raising
88	`FeatureDisabledError` (REQ-193), mapped by `src/lib/errors.ts` to a
89	`forbidden` `AppErrorShape` carrying the flag key in `meta`.
90	
91	## Consequences
92	
93	**What this buys the team.** `isEnabled()` being the single function called
94	by both server gates and the client snapshot means the two can never
95	disagree — the exact failure mode (a rendered control the server then
96	rejects) the team set out to prevent is structurally impossible as long as
97	nothing calls the strategy logic directly. Adding a new flag is declarative:
98	a new entry in `FEATURE_FLAG_DEFINITIONS` with the right strategy kind, no
99	new code path. `bucketOf()`'s determinism turned out to matter more than
100	anticipated once `ai_issue_summary` shipped — Ada Whitfield's rollout plan
101	depended on being able to tell a specific pilot customer "you're in the 25
102	percent," true for their whole organization consistently, which a
103	per-request random roll could never have promised. `webhooks` being both
104	plan-gated and explicitly non-overridable closed a real gap: without the
105	`overridable: false` flag, a support engineer adding an org to an override
106	list to unblock one customer's early access could have accidentally granted
107	a feature (webhooks) that has its own resourcing implications (ADR-011's
108	`webhook:deliver` rate-limit bucket, ADR-018's delivery infrastructure) that
109	a simple UI toggle was never meant to provision.
110	
111	**What it costs.** Four strategy kinds mean `isEnabled()`'s switch statement
112	is the one place that has to stay correct for all of them simultaneously,
113	and a flag's evaluation now depends on the shape of `FlagContext` being
114	fully and correctly populated by every caller — a caller that forgets to
115	set `ctx.role` when checking a role-gated flag, or `ctx.plan` for a
116	plan-gated one, silently gets `false` from the relevant strategy branch
117	rather than an error, which is safe (fails closed) but has caused at least
118	one debugging session (February 2026, `issue_templates` appearing
119	unavailable for an admin) that traced back to a call site building
120	`FlagContext` from a stale actor object missing the current role. The
121	percentage strategy's hash-based bucketing is also opaque to manual
122	reasoning — there is no way to look at an org's id and immediately know
123	which bucket it falls in without running `bucketOf()`, which has occasionally
124	made support conversations ("why does this specific customer have AI
125	summaries and this one doesn't") require an engineer to run the function
126	rather than answer from memory.
127	
128	## Alternatives considered
129	
130	**Separate, purpose-built mechanisms per gating type** — a plan-check helper
131	for plan gates, a role-check helper for role gates, a dedicated rollout
132	service for percentage flags. This is roughly where the codebase started
133	before this ADR, in an earlier prototype of `kanban_board`'s gating. Rejected
134	for the same reason ADR-003 rejects per-resource permission guards: no single
135	evaluator, no single place the client and server can both call to guarantee
136	agreement.
137	
138	**A third-party feature-flag SaaS.** The default choice at many companies,
139	and rejected immediately given the no-external-services constraint — there is
140	nowhere for a flag-evaluation SDK to phone home to in this build.
141	
142	**True random percentage rollout** (roll the dice on every request rather
143	than hashing to a stable bucket). Rejected specifically because it fails
144	REQ-189's determinism requirement and would have made the pilot-customer
145	rollout scenario impossible to promise reliably — a flickering feature is
146	worse for a rollout than a slower one.
147	
148	## References
149	
150	- REQ-185 (flags declared in a single registry), REQ-186 (evaluation goes
151	  through one function), REQ-187 (four evaluation strategies), REQ-189
152	  (percentage rollout deterministic per organization), REQ-190 (some flags
153	  not overridable), REQ-191 (per-organization overrides in organization
154	  settings), REQ-193 (disabled feature fails with `FeatureDisabledError`),
155	  REQ-194 (client receives a snapshot, not the registry), REQ-195 (flag keys
156	  are a closed union)
157	- ADR-003 (the single-entry-point pattern this evaluator mirrors), ADR-010
158	  (`PLAN_ORDER`/`planAtLeast` the plan strategy reads from)
159	- Code: `src/config/feature-flags.ts` (`FEATURE_FLAG_DEFINITIONS`,
160	  `FEATURE_FLAG_KEYS`, `getFlagDefinition`, `isFeatureFlagKey`),
161	  `src/lib/feature-flags.ts` (`isEnabled`, `snapshotFlags`, `assertEnabled`,
162	  `FeatureDisabledError`, `bucketOf`), `src/types/feature-flag.ts`
163

percent," true for their whole organization consistently, which a
per-request random roll could never have promised. `webhooks` being both
plan-gated and explicitly non-overridable closed a real gap: without the
`overridable: false` flag, a support engineer adding an org to an override
list to unblock one customer's early access could have accidentally granted
a feature (webhooks) that has its own resourcing implications (ADR-011's
`webhook:deliver` rate-limit bucket, ADR-018's delivery infrastructure) that
a simple UI toggle was never meant to provision.

**What it costs.** Four strategy kinds mean `isEnabled()`'s switch statement
is the one place that has to stay correct for all of them simultaneously,
and a flag's evaluation now depends on the shape of `FlagContext` being
fully and correctly populated by every caller — a caller that forgets to
set `ctx.role` when checking a role-gated flag, or `ctx.plan` for a
plan-gated one, silently gets `false` from the relevant strategy branch
rather than an error, which is safe (fails closed) but has caused at least
one debugging session (February 2026, `issue_templates` appearing
unavailable for an admin) that traced back to a call site building
`FlagContext` from a stale actor object missing the current role. The
percentage strategy's hash-based bucketing is also opaque to manual
reasoning — there is no way to look at an org's id and immediately know
which bucket it falls in without running `bucketOf()`, which has occasionally
made support conversations ("why does this specific customer have AI
summaries and this one doesn't") require an engineer to run the function
rather than answer from memory.

## Alternatives considered

**Separate, purpose-built mechanisms per gating type** — a plan-check helper
for plan gates, a role-check helper for role gates, a dedicated rollout
service for percentage flags. This is roughly where the codebase started
before this ADR, in an earlier prototype of `kanban_board`'s gating. Rejected
for the same reason ADR-003 rejects per-resource permission guards: no single
evaluator, no single place the client and server can both call to guarantee
agreement.

**A third-party feature-flag SaaS.** The default choice at many companies,
and rejected immediately given the no-external-services constraint — there is
nowhere for a flag-evaluation SDK to phone home to in this build.

**True random percentage rollout** (roll the dice on every request rather
than hashing to a stable bucket). Rejected specifically because it fails
REQ-189's determinism requirement and would have made the pilot-customer
rollout scenario impossible to promise reliably — a flickering feature is
worse for a rollout than a slower one.

## References

- REQ-185 (flags declared in a single registry), REQ-186 (evaluation goes
  through one function), REQ-187 (four evaluation strategies), REQ-189
  (percentage rollout deterministic per organization), REQ-190 (some flags
  not overridable), REQ-191 (per-organization overrides in organization
  settings), REQ-193 (disabled feature fails with `FeatureDisabledError`),
  REQ-194 (client receives a snapshot, not the registry), REQ-195 (flag keys
  are a closed union)
- ADR-003 (the single-entry-point pattern this evaluator mirrors), ADR-010
  (`PLAN_ORDER`/`planAtLeast` the plan strategy reads from)
- Code: `src/config/feature-flags.ts` (`FEATURE_FLAG_DEFINITIONS`,
  `FEATURE_FLAG_KEYS`, `getFlagDefinition`, `isFeatureFlagKey`),
  `src/lib/feature-flags.ts` (`isEnabled`, `snapshotFlags`, `assertEnabled`,
  `FeatureDisabledError`, `bucketOf`), `src/types/feature-flag.ts`

1	---
2	title: Notes — plan ladder pricing
3	id: OPS-NOTES-2026-02-10
4	status: approved
5	owners: [r.saito]
6	last_updated: 2026-02-10
7	related: [ADR-010, REQ-131, REQ-132]
8	---
9	
10	**Date:** 2026-02-10
11	**Attendees:** r.saito (chair), a.whitfield, d.okafor, m.lindqvist
12	
13	## Agenda
14	
15	1. Finalize the four-plan ladder's numeric limits ahead of `PLAN_LIMITS` being frozen in
16	   code.
17	2. Decide the `enterprise` plan's price and whether any dimension should stay
18	   unlimited versus a large finite number.
19	3. Discuss the `UNLIMITED` representation and whether `Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY` is
20	   actually safe to use in downstream arithmetic.
21	
22	## Discussion
23	
24	Rin presented the draft ladder: `free` (3 seats, 2 projects, 100 issues per project, 100
25	MB storage, 100 API requests/hour, 0 webhooks, 30-day retention, $0), `starter` (10/10/
26	1000/2000/1000/2/90/$900 per seat monthly), `growth` (50/100/10000/20000/10000/10/365/
27	$1900), and `enterprise` (unlimited seats, projects, and issues per project, 500000 MB
28	storage, 100000 API requests/hour, unlimited webhooks, 2555-day retention, $3900).
29	
30	Ada pushed back on `enterprise` webhooks being unlimited rather than a large finite
31	number, worried that "unlimited webhooks" as a literal product claim could be abused by
32	a single enterprise customer registering thousands of endpoints and degrading the shared
33	webhook delivery pipeline for everyone — a concern that, in hindsight after
34	`postmortem-2026-04-17-webhook-backlog.md`, turned out to be prescient about
35	throughput risk generally, even though that incident was triggered by event volume
36	rather than endpoint count specifically. The group discussed capping enterprise
37	webhooks at a large finite number like 500 instead. Deji argued that from an engineering
38	standpoint, "unlimited" and "500" require the same code — a numeric comparison against
39	`getPlanLimits(plan).webhooks` either way — so the decision was really a product and
40	sales question, not a technical one. Ada ultimately kept `enterprise` webhooks unlimited
41	for the sales narrative, but the group logged the throughput risk as a topic to revisit
42	if it ever becomes a real operational problem, which is exactly what happened three
43	months later.
44	
45	Mira raised the `UNLIMITED = Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY` representation directly: is it
46	actually safe everywhere a limit is compared or used arithmetically? The group walked
47	through `wouldExceedLimit(plan, resource, used, requested)` — comparing `used +
48	requested > limit` — and confirmed that `POSITIVE_INFINITY` behaves correctly there,
49	since any finite `used + requested` is always less than infinity. Deji flagged one
50	subtlety: `retentionDays` being used in date arithmetic (`now - retentionDays *
51	MS_PER_DAY` in the cleanup job) means `retentionDays` should never itself be
52	`UNLIMITED`, because that would produce `NaN` in the resulting timestamp — the group
53	confirmed enterprise's retention is deliberately a large finite number (2555 days, seven
54	years) rather than infinite, specifically to avoid this. This became a documented
55	convention: `UNLIMITED` is safe for count-based quotas compared with `>`, but any limit
56	that feeds date or duration arithmetic must stay finite.
57	
58	Ada and Rin spent the remainder of the meeting on pricing itself, which is recorded
59	here for completeness even though it is less an engineering decision than a business
60	one: `starter` at $900/seat/month, `growth` at $1900/seat/month, `enterprise` at
61	$3900/seat/month, all stored as integer cents (`priceCentsPerSeatMonthly`) to avoid
62	floating-point rounding in billing calculations — Deji was firm on this point, noting
63	that any prior experience with float-based money fields eventually produces a support
64	ticket about a one-cent discrepancy that takes an afternoon to track down.
65	
66	## Decisions
67	
68	1. The four-plan ladder ships with the numeric limits as drafted above (relates
69	   `REQ-131`, `REQ-132`).
70	2. `enterprise` webhooks remain unlimited (`Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY`) for the sales
71	   narrative, with the throughput risk explicitly logged as a known trade-off rather than
72	   silently accepted.
73	3. `UNLIMITED` is safe for count-based quota comparisons but must never be used for a
74	   limit that feeds date/duration arithmetic; `retentionDays` stays finite even on
75	   `enterprise` (2555 days).
76	4. All prices are stored as integer cents (`priceCentsPerSeatMonthly`), never floats.
77	
78	Deji raised one more question near the close of the meeting: should the seat count
79	displayed to a customer include the owner, or is the owner counted separately from
80	"seats"? The group confirmed the owner is counted as one of the org's seats like any
81	other active member — there is no separate, uncounted "founder" slot — and that this
82	should be stated explicitly in customer-facing plan comparison copy, since a customer
83	mentally modeling "seats" as "additional people beyond myself" would undercount by one
84	and be surprised when an invite fails sooner than expected. Ada agreed to fold this into
85	the same messaging pass covering integer-cents billing precision, rather than treating
86	it as a separate documentation task.
87	
88	## Follow-ups
89	
90	- Ada to note the enterprise-webhooks throughput risk in the internal sales-engineering
91	  handbook so a large prospective customer's webhook usage pattern gets flagged before
92	  contract signing, not after.
93	- Deji to add a code comment on `PlanLimits` documenting the "safe for counts, unsafe for
94	  durations" rule about `UNLIMITED`, so a future contributor adding a new limited
95	  resource does not accidentally make a duration field unlimited.
96	- Rin to confirm with finance that integer-cents pricing matches how invoices are
97	  actually generated downstream (`REQ-143`).
98

## Agenda

1. Finalize the four-plan ladder's numeric limits ahead of `PLAN_LIMITS` being frozen in

2. Decide the `enterprise` plan's price and whether any dimension should stay
   unlimited versus a large finite number.
3. Discuss the `UNLIMITED` representation and whether `Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY` is
   actually safe to use in downstream arithmetic.

## Discussion

Rin presented the draft ladder: `free` (3 seats, 2 projects, 100 issues per project, 100
MB storage, 100 API requests/hour, 0 webhooks, 30-day retention, $0), `starter` (10/10/
1000/2000/1000/2/90/$900 per seat monthly), `growth` (50/100/10000/20000/10000/10/365/
$1900), and `enterprise` (unlimited seats, projects, and issues per project, 500000 MB
storage, 100000 API requests/hour, unlimited webhooks, 2555-day retention, $3900).

Ada pushed back on `enterprise` webhooks being unlimited rather than a large finite
number, worried that "unlimited webhooks" as a literal product claim could be abused by
a single enterprise customer registering thousands of endpoints and degrading the shared
webhook delivery pipeline for everyone — a concern that, in hindsight after
`postmortem-2026-04-17-webhook-backlog.md`, turned out to be prescient about
throughput risk generally, even though that incident was triggered by event volume
rather than endpoint count specifically. The group discussed capping enterprise
webhooks at a large finite number like 500 instead. Deji argued that from an engineering
standpoint, "unlimited" and "500" require the same code — a numeric comparison against
`getPlanLimits(plan).webhooks` either way — so the decision was really a product and
sales question, not a technical one. Ada ultimately kept `enterprise` webhooks unlimited
for the sales narrative, but the group logged the throughput risk as a topic to revisit
if it ever becomes a real operational problem, which is exactly what happened three
months later.

Mira raised the `UNLIMITED = Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY` representation directly: is it
actually safe everywhere a limit is compared or used arithmetically? The group walked
through `wouldExceedLimit(plan, resource, used, requested)` — comparing `used +
requested > limit` — and confirmed that `POSITIVE_INFINITY` behaves correctly there,
since any finite `used + requested` is always less than infinity. Deji flagged one
subtlety: `retentionDays` being used in date arithmetic (`now - retentionDays *
MS_PER_DAY` in the cleanup job) means `retentionDays` should never itself be
`UNLIMITED`, because that would produce `NaN` in the resulting timestamp — the group
confirmed enterprise's retention is deliberately a large finite number (2555 days, seven
years) rather than infinite, specifically to avoid this. This became a documented
convention: `UNLIMITED` is safe for count-based quotas compared with `>`, but any limit
that feeds date or duration arithmetic must stay finite.

Ada and Rin spent the remainder of the meeting on pricing itself, which is recorded
here for completeness even though it is less an engineering decision than a business
one: `starter` at $900/seat/month, `growth` at $1900/seat/month, `enterprise` at
$3900/seat/month, all stored as integer cents (`priceCentsPerSeatMonthly`) to avoid
floating-point rounding in billing calculations — Deji was firm on this point, noting
that any prior experience with float-based money fields eventually produces a support
ticket about a one-cent discrepancy that takes an afternoon to track down.

## Decisions

1. The four-plan ladder ships with the numeric limits as drafted above (relates
   `REQ-131`, `REQ-132`).
2. `enterprise` webhooks remain unlimited (`Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY`) for the sales
   narrative, with the throughput risk explicitly logged as a known trade-off rather than
   silently accepted.
3. `UNLIMITED` is safe for count-based quota comparisons but must never be used for a
   limit that feeds date/duration arithmetic; `retentionDays` stays finite even on
   `enterprise` (2555 days).
4. All prices are stored as integer cents (`priceCentsPerSeatMonthly`), never floats.

Deji raised one more question near the close of the meeting: should the seat count
displayed to a customer include the owner, or is the owner counted separately from
"seats"? The group confirmed the owner is counted as one of the org's seats like any
other active member — there is no separate, uncounted "founder" slot — and that this
should be stated explicitly in customer-facing plan comparison copy, since a customer
mentally modeling "seats" as "additional people beyond myself" would undercount by one
and be surprised when an invite fails sooner than expected. Ada agreed to fold this into
the same messaging pass covering integer-cents billing precision, rather than treating
it as a separate documentation task.

## Follow-ups

- Ada to note the enterprise-webhooks throughput risk in the internal sales-engineering
  handbook so a large prospective customer's webhook usage pattern gets flagged before
  contract signing, not after.
- Deji to add a code comment on `PlanLimits` documenting the "safe for counts, unsafe for
  durations" rule about `UNLIMITED`, so a future contributor adding a new limited
  resource does not accidentally make a duration field unlimited.
- Rin to confirm with finance that integer-cents pricing matches how invoices are
  actually generated downstream (`REQ-143`).

### REQ-134 — Project count is checked before project creation

- **Priority:** must
- **Status:** implemented
- **Related:** REQ-043, REQ-044
- **Implemented by:** `src/server/services/billing-service.ts` — `checkLimit`, `assertWithinLimit`
- **Verified by:** `tests/services/billing-service.test.ts`, `tests/contract/plan-limits.test.ts`

The ladder for this particular quota is 3 projects on `free`, 10 on `starter`, 100 on
`growth` and unlimited on `enterprise`. The free tier's allowance was picked to be enough
for a team to model a real workflow — a project each for the product, the platform and the
website — without giving away enough capacity to serve a working agency.

This document is the canonical statement of the rule `REQ-043` in `projects.md` implements:
`checkLimit(orgId, 'projects', used)` must return a non-exceeding verdict before
`insertProject` runs, using `countProjects` with its default scope that includes archived
projects (`REQ-044`).

**Acceptance criteria**

13	evaluation function, the four rollout strategies, plan gating, non-overridable flags,

28	`getSnapshot`/`toggleFlag` for the settings page and its Server Action.

31	general rules engine: plan-gated (the flag is on once the org's plan reaches a threshold,
32	per `PLAN_ORDER`), percentage rollout (deterministic per organization, not per user, so a
33	whole organization sees consistent behavior rather than individual members randomly
34	diverging), boolean-always-on (`command_palette`), and role-gated (the flag is on once the
35	acting user's role reaches a threshold, used by `issue_templates`). Every flag in the
36	registry declares exactly one of these strategies plus whether it is `overridable`.
37	
38	Ten flags exist today: `kanban_board` (plan >= starter, overridable), `ai_issue_summary`
39	(percentage 25, overridable), `command_palette` (always on, not overridable),
40	`activity_feed` (plan >= growth, overridable), `public_projects` (plan >= enterprise,
41	overridable), `webhooks` (plan >= growth, not overridable), `csv_export` (plan >= starter,
42	overridable), `digest_email` (plan >= growth, overridable), `issue_templates` (role >=
43	admin, overridable), and `advanced_search` (plan >= enterprise, overridable). `webhooks` and
44	`command_palette` are the only two flags marked not overridable — for `command_palette`
45	because there is no reason to ever turn off a zero-cost client affordance, and for
46	`webhooks` because the plan-tier gate on webhooks is a monetization boundary the product
47	team does not want individual support interactions to erode by ad hoc override.
48	
49	Organization-level overrides live in `Organization.settings` (`REQ-005`, defined in
50	`organizations.md`), which is why this document does not restate the storage location but
51	does define the override's evaluation semantics: an override only takes effect for flags
52	whose definition marks them `overridable`, and `toggleFlag` — the only mutator — requires
53	`org:manage_flags`, whose `ROLE_MATRIX` minimum is `admin`.
54	
55	`src/config/nav.ts`'s `visibleNav` is a second, independent consumer of the flag system worth
56	naming here even though it belongs conceptually to navigation rather than to flags: each
57	`NavItem` optionally names both a `PermissionAction` and a `FeatureFlagKey`, and `visibleNav`

59	for every item, so a flagged-off feature's settings link disappears from navigation the same
